title: How to Set Up an AI Hedge Fund in MetaTrader 5
text:
The previous article
ended with an honest admission: a system consisting of several analysts is a good start, but it is not the end of the conversation. The council demonstrated that several voices are better than one, but even fifteen voices working together on a single pair still amount to a small room.
Imagine the management committee of a real fund. Ten analysts with fundamentally different philosophies are sitting at the same table. Victor focuses solely on the trend and the alignment of moving averages — for him, a price above the MA50 is already sufficient grounds for a BUY. Dmitry, who holds three PhDs, calculates the z-score for the deviation from the Bollinger midline and will not generate a signal until that number crosses the 0.8 threshold. Chen does not react to anything without volume confirmation. Yuki’s primary focus is the body of the last candle, almost to the exclusion of everything else. Seated at a separate table are four risk managers, each with their own independent “axes of fear”: one measures the ATR, the second evaluates entry timing, the third assesses market regime quality, and the fourth looks for tail events. And presiding over them all is the Chairman, who reads all fourteen reports and enforces a strict three-step voting procedure.
Now multiply that by eight. Eight currency pairs, eight isolated councils, eight independent reputation engines — all within a single Python process.
That is exactly what this article describes.
Why One Pair Was Not Enough
The previous architecture operated on a single trading symbol. This meant that the system had a blind spot the size of the entire rest of the market.
Currencies move in correlation with one another. EURUSD and GBPUSD often move in tandem because both are exposed to dollar risk. USDJPY behaves like a safe-haven asset during times of panic. XAUUSD is a completely different beast with its own seasonal patterns and reaction to inflation. An analyst who trades only EURUSD and doesn't see what is happening with the yen is working with one eye closed.
But it's not just about correlations. Different currency pairs offer different numbers of trading opportunities depending on the market regime. When EURUSD is stuck in a narrow range and the council of fifteen keeps saying HOLD over and over, GBPUSD may at that same time be in a clean trend, with seven analysts voting BUY and zero BLOCKED. A system that can listen to only one voice of the market misses out on everything else.
The solution is obvious: run eight isolated councils in parallel. Each one works on its own pair, with its own reputation history, PnL targets, and motivational state.
Architecture: One Process, Eight Worlds
The technical core of the system is the PortContext class. This is an isolated state container for a single currency pair:
class
PortContext:
"""Isolated context for a single port (a single currency pair)."""
def
__init__(self, port:
int
, pair:
str
):
        self.port         = port
        self.pair         = pair
        self.reputation   = ReputationEngine()
# its own reputation engine
self.chat_history = []
# its own chat history
self.history_lock = threading.Lock()
Eight PortContext instances are created at startup and exist independently. Victor's reputation on EURUSD has no effect on his reputation on XAUUSD. The fund’s daily hunger for the yen does not make the franc council any less demanding. Each pair is a world of its own.

No averaging, trailing, or session filter parameters. The Expert Advisor does one thing: it listens to the council of fifteen and opens or closes a position.
Ten Analysts: A Gallery of Philosophies
The selection of participants for the first phase is not arbitrary. Each one represents a distinct trading school with its own logic and its own blind spots. It is precisely the mismatch between these blind spots that creates the ensemble's value.
Victor
is a trend trader. A BUY signal if the price is above the MA20 or MA50 with positive momentum. A SELL signal is symmetric. NO SIGNAL — only when the momentum is perfectly flat. He never argues with himself — he always sides with the stronger argument.
Maria
is a contrarian bear with strong convictions. She looks for SELL first and foremost. An RSI above 65 and the price at the upper Bollinger Band — that is enough for her. When the market is oversold, she can issue a BUY signal. Her value lies in shouting “Stop!” precisely when everyone else is shouting “Go!”
Elena
is a specialist in mean reversion. She operates only at extremes: a touch of the lower band with RSI7 below 35 means BUY. A touch of the upper band with RSI7 above 65 means SELL. Near the middle band, she uses the direction of the latest momentum. NO SIGNAL only in the RSI7 dead zone from 45 to 55, strictly at the middle band.
Dmitry
is a quant with a PhD. Calculates the z-score: z = (price − BB_mid) / StdDev. Z above 0.8 means SELL. Below −0.8 means BUY. Between zero and 0.8, he looks at momentum. Shows the math in the answer.
Chen
is an expert on volume and microstructure. A Volume Ratio above 1.2 plus a bullish candle means BUY. Plus a bearish candle means SELL. When volume is low, he focuses on the direction of the candle. NO SIGNAL — only when volume is below 0.5× the average and there is a perfect doji.
Isabella
is a volatility trader. Volatility expansion within an uptrend — BUY. In a downtrend — SELL. When volatility contracts, she trades in the direction of the trend. NO SIGNAL — only when both the trend and volatility are perfectly neutral at the same time.
Marcus
is a Wyckoff analyst. Looks for a spring (a false breakout to the downside followed by a reversal) or an upthrust (a false breakout to the upside followed by a rejection). In the absence of a clear Wyckoff event, he follows the trend. He can read the footprints of institutional money.
Yuki
is a Japanese candlestick expert. A bullish candle with a body larger than 0.3 ATR — BUY. A bearish candle under the same condition — SELL. With a small body, she checks its position: near the lower band it gives a BUY, near the upper band she gives a SELL; otherwise, she follows momentum. NO SIGNAL — only on a perfect doji with a body less than 0.1 ATR, strictly at the middle band.
Raphael
is an expert on divergences. All momentum indicators are pointing upward—BUY. Down — SELL. When signals are mixed: the majority (2/3) determines the direction. NO SIGNAL — only on a perfect 50/50 split. Its signals are strongest when all the oscillators are in sync.
Sophie
is a systematic trader. Counts binary checks: is the price above MA20? Is RSI14 above 50? Is Stochastic %K above %D? That makes ten questions in all. Five or more bullish answers — BUY. Five or more bearish answers — SELL. In the event of a tie, the last candle decides.
In the code, each analyst is a system prompt in the BASE_ANALYST_PROMPTS dictionary:
BASE_ANALYST_PROMPTS = {
"victor"
: (
"You are VICTOR STONE — momentum master. Trend is God. Indecision kills returns. "
"Signal BUY if price > MA20 OR MA50 with positive momentum. "
"Signal SELL if price < MA20 OR MA50 with negative momentum. "
"If trend is ambiguous, pick the STRONGER side. NO SIGNAL only if momentum is perfectly flat. "
"Name EXACT values. Reply: BUY/SELL/NO SIGNAL in 3 sharp sentences. No JSON."
),
"dmitri"
: (
"You are DMITRI VOLKOV — head quant, PhD x3. Models demand action. "
"Compute: z = (price - BB_mid) / StdDev. "
"z > 0.8 = SELL. z < -0.8 = BUY. 0 < z < 0.8: check momentum — if positive = BUY, negative = SELL. "
"Show your math. BUY/SELL/NO SIGNAL. 3 sentences. No JSON."
),
"sophie"
: (
"You are SOPHIE LAURENT — systematic signal counter. Numbers never lie. "
"Count BUL vs BEA signals across all indicators. "
"Score >= 5 BUL = BUY. Score >= 5 BEA = SELL. Tie: use last candle direction. "
"Show EXACT count. 3 sentences. No JSON."
),
#
... the remaining seven
}
Note: each prompt ends with "No JSON." Analysts speak in free-form text. Only the Chairman is required to respond in JSON, because only the Chairman's response is parsed programmatically.
Four Risk Axes
Risk managers aren't just voices of caution. Each of the four looks at an independent dimension of market risk.
Alexey
— volatility and ATR. The blocking threshold has been raised to ATR% > 0.6% (in v3 it was 0.3% — v4 is more aggressive). BB width above 1.0% — HIGH. 0.5–1.0% — CAUTION. Below 0.4% — APPROVED. Prefers APPROVED whenever there is any doubt.
Helena
— entry timing. Candle body greater than 1.2× ATR (it was 0.8 in v3) — the entry is late, BLOCKED. Stochastic above 92 or below 8 (in v3 it was 85/15) — BLOCKED. Standard overbought conditions are CAUTION only, not BLOCKED. Prefers CAUTION over BLOCKED.
James
— market regime quality. 4 out of 5 moving averages are aligned — APPROVED. 3 out of 5 — at most CAUTION. Fewer than 2 out of 5 — BLOCKED. Blocking requires two or more conflicting signals.
Natalia
— black swans. Blocks only on true tail events: RSI7 below 10 or above 90 (in v3 it was 15/85), Volume Ratio above 3.0 (in v3 it was 2.0), ATR14 above 1.5×ATR21 (in v3 it was 1.3). Moderate extremes are CAUTION only.
RISK_PROMPTS = {
    "alexei": (
        "You are ALEXEI STORM — Volatility Risk Officer. "
        "ATR% > 0.6 = HIGH RISK → BLOCKED. ATR% 0.4-0.6 = CAUTION. Below 0.4 = APPROVED. "
        "BB width > 1.0% = HIGH. 0.5-1.0% = CAUTION. Prefer APPROVED unless extremes are clear. "
        "VERDICT: APPROVED/CAUTION/BLOCKED. 2 sentences. No JSON."

Note the intentional relaxation of blocking thresholds compared to v3. This is not accidental — it is a decision. In v4, the system operates more actively: the market always has a direction, and the risk managers' job is to block only truly dangerous situations, not everything indiscriminately.

Chairman and Voting Procedure
The Chairman’s prompt is not just a description of the role; it is a hard-coded procedure with specific numerical conditions:

Note: the voting threshold `vote_threshold` is a parameter, not a constant. It is calculated dynamically depending on the state of the reputation engine:
def
get_weighted_vote_threshold(self) ->
int
:
if
self.aggression_mode:
return
4
# the fund is critically hungry — we lower the bar
if
self.hunger_level >
0.4
:
return
5
# moderate hunger
return
6
# standard mode
In standard mode, six analysts are needed. In aggressive mode, four are needed. The same market setup will produce a different response depending on how far the fund has met its daily targets.
Reputation Engine: Who Has Earned Trust
Each pair has its own ReputationEngine. Each analyst starts with a reputation of 50.0, which changes based on trading results:
REWARD_CORRECT      = +
8.0
# correct prediction
REWARD_CORRECT_BIG  = +
15.0
# large profitable prediction (PnL > threshold)
PENALTY_WRONG       = -
6.0
# incorrect prediction
PENALTY_WRONG_BIG   = -
12.0
# large losing prediction
REWARD_STREAK_BONUS = +
3.0
# bonus for a streak of 3+ correct predictions in a row
PENALTY_STREAK_MULT =
1.5
# penalty multiplier for a streak of 3+ errors
REPUTATION_DECAY    =
0.995
# gradual reputation decay each cycle
The REPUTATION_DECAY parameter, set to 0.995, is important. Each cycle, reputation is multiplied by 0.995. Without this, an analyst who scored 90 points in the first month would remain dominant forever — even if the market regime changed and their methodology stopped working. Reputation decay forces an analyst to constantly prove their relevance.
In addition to decay, a background daemon runs every 15 minutes:

Up to that point, the Council of 15 architecture had looked convincing as a concept: ten analysts with decorrelated philosophies, four risk managers with independent axes of assessment, a Chair manwith a strict voting procedure, and a reputation engine that remembers who made mistakes. But in trading, architecture is worthless on its own if it cannot be run through the ruthless machine of facts — the Strategy Tester. That is where the beautiful diagrams end and the only conversation that matters begins.

Over eight weeks, the system executed 59 trades and earned USD 2,471 on a USD 10,000 deposit. A Profit Factor of 2.09 means that for every dollar lost, the system generated two dollars. That is a strong metric.
A Sharpe Ratio of 6.31 is not a typo. For comparison, professional hedge funds consider a Sharpe Ratio above 1.0 a good result, and above 2.0 an excellent one. The value of 6.31 is explained by a combination of two factors: a high win rate (64%) together with very low volatility of results — the longest losing streak was only 2 trades in a row. The system did not experience any prolonged drawdowns.
LR Correlation 0.97 — the correlation coefficient between the equity curve and a straight line. A value close to 1.0 indicates that the deposit grew steadily, without any sharp drops or spikes. It was not a case of “making all the money in three days and then sitting on it,” but rather steady growth week after week.
The Recovery Factor of 6.16 indicates that the system earned 6.16 times more than the maximum drawdown. With a drawdown of USD 401, the profit was USD 2471. That is a good ratio.
The clean architecture of the Expert Advisor makes it possible to clearly separate the sources of exits:
By Take Profit — 29 trades (49%)
. Nearly half of the trades reached their target level. This means that the council quite often issued signals in the right direction with sufficient confidence — the position had time to move 300 points before an opposite signal arrived.
On an opposite signal from the council — 24 trades (41%)
. Four out of ten trades were closed not by TP/SL, but because the Chairman changed direction. This is a key feature of the system: it does not mechanically wait for a stop order to trigger, but reacts to changes in the market picture. Some of these exits are early profit-taking, while others are a way to avoid a loss that would otherwise have reached the stop loss (SL).
By Stop Loss — 6 trades (10%)
. Only one in ten trades reached the hard stop. This suggests that, in most cases, the council’s opposite signal came before the price reached the stop loss (SL). The risk managers and the Chairman managed to notice the change in the market picture before the loss became maximum.
Breakdown by direction: shorts — 36 trades with a win rate of 66.67%; longs — 23 trades with a win rate of 60.87%. The bearish bias during that period (October–November 2025 on EUR/USD) coincided with the system performing more accurately on sell trades.
The average position holding time is 14 hours and 1 minute. With an H1 timeframe and analysis every 6 hours, that is roughly 2–3 new bars before the next request to the council. The system does not scalp — it holds positions across several trading sessions.
The minimum time in a trade is 1 hour and 6 minutes. These are instances where an opposite signal arrived on the very next bar. The maximum is 69 hours and 16 minutes — almost three days. Positions held for such a long time are typical of cases where the council consistently maintained the same direction over several analysis cycles.
The maximum losing streak is 2 in a row. Over the course of eight weeks and 59 trades, the system never recorded three consecutive losses. The average losing streak is 1. This is a direct consequence of the fact that when the stop loss is triggered, the system immediately readjusts: a loss most often means that the market context has changed, and the next request to the council already produces a different signal.

Confirmed

A high win rate with minimal losing streaks suggests that filtering through four independent risk managers is working: the system really does admit fewer bad entries than a single algorithm would.

The system's behavior under reduced aggressiveness has also not been tested: in the test, the voting threshold dynamically dropped to 4 when the fund was hungry. How often this occurred and how it affected signal quality is a separate issue that warrants analysis.
Backtest results are not proof that the system will work in the future. This is a sufficient basis for the next step: forward testing on a demo account with real API latency.
An Honest Conversation About Limitations
A fifteen-vote system is impressive. This impression needs to be deliberately tempered.
All fifteen participants are the same grok-3-fast model with different system prompts. Their independence refers to the independence of their perspectives, not the independence of the neural network's weights. If the base model is systematically wrong about a specific market pattern, all fifteen “analysts” will be wrong there at the same time. The consensus of fifteen copies of a single model is not the same as the consensus of fifteen independently trained models.
The second limitation is parallelism across eight currency pairs. When processing eight symbols simultaneously, the system makes up to 14 parallel API calls per pair — that is, up to 112 requests in a single analysis cycle. You need to understand which pricing plan can handle that kind of load.
Third: reputation memory is limited to the current process session. When the Python server is restarted, all reputation scores are reset to 50.0. The solution is persistent storage (SQLite) — that is the next step.
Fourth: the Expert Advisor does not know what happened after the previous signal. Every decision is made in a vacuum, based only on the last 100 price bars. The system does not see that a week ago, with a similar vote configuration, the Chairman turned out to be wrong. This is precisely the main argument in favor of the next step: equipping the system with long-term memory and a mechanism for evaluating the quality of its own decisions based on historical data.
Conclusion
We started with just one voice. Previous articles have shown that four voices with different roles produce a qualitatively different result. This article took the next step: fifteen voices with fundamentally different philosophies, operating in parallel across eight currency pairs with isolated reputation engines and a motivational system.
Technically, this is a direct extension of the previous version. The same Python architecture, the same WebSocket protocol, and the same technical indicators built entirely on NumPy. New features include multi-port support, eight isolated contexts, a reputation engine with feedback, and a motivational context that makes voting thresholds dynamic rather than fixed.
The AIHedgeFund_v4_clean.mq5 Expert Advisor has been intentionally stripped of any unnecessary mechanics: no averaging, no trailing, and no partial closing. Only the council signal, SL, TP, and exit on an opposite signal. This makes it possible to evaluate the quality of the AI decisions themselves, without the added complexity of additional logic.
The result is not just a BUY, SELL, or HOLD recommendation; it is the transcript of a professional investment committee meeting featuring ten specialists, four risk managers, and one Chairman. Every vote is identified by name, every argument is recorded in the log, and every risk-manager veto is backed up by specific numbers.

The dynamic vote_threshold is computed as: 4 in aggressive mode, 5 in moderate hunger (>0.4), 6 otherwise — directly tied to measurable fund PnL state.

against: The trading signal depends on the Chairman's decision, which is generated by an LLM (grok-3-fast) parsing free-form natural language outputs from analysts and risk managers — the article provides no deterministic, formulaic rule for how BUY/SELL/HOLD is derived from inputs; it only describes a high-level voting-and-weighting architecture with dynamic thresholds and motivational context, but no exact, reproducible condition (e.g., no precise mathematical or logical expression that maps indicator values → final signal without LLM interpretation)

The system relies on LLM-generated opinions (e.g., 'Dmitri computes z-score... z > 0.8 = SELL') — but the actual output is free-form text ('BUY/SELL/NO SIGNAL in 3 sharp sentences. No JSON.'), and the parsing of those responses into structured votes is not specified: the article says analysts 'speak in free-form text' and only the Chairman's response is parsed programmatically, yet the vote tallying step (_tally_analysts) is left undefined — no formula, no regex pattern, no validation logic is given for extracting 'BUY' from unstructured prose

The Chairman’s decision logic includes dynamic, state-dependent conditions (e.g., 'STEP 1 — RISK GATE: • 4 BLOCKED → "hold"', '• 3 BLOCKED → "hold" unless analyst consensus is overwhelming (9+)', 'aggression mode lowers threshold to 4') — but the definition of 'overwhelming (9+)' and the mapping from risk verdict counts + weighted vote counts + motivational state to final signal is embedded in the LLM’s system prompt, not codified as a testable, deterministic rule; the prompt says 'Reply ONLY with JSON', but the *generation* of that JSON is delegated to an LLM, not a fixed algorithm
non_fatal: No backtest is shown for other pairs beyond EURUSD (H1, Oct–Nov 2025), so generalizability across the claimed eight pairs is unverified.
No out-of-sample test is reported — the backtest period is short (8 weeks) and not split into in-sample/out-of-sample.
Latency (10–17 sec per cycle) makes the system unsuitable for M1 or even M5 timeframes, but this is a performance limitation, not a fatal flaw in the rule definition.

The system uses WebSocket API calls to an external LLM (grok-3-fast), implying dependency on external infrastructure and non-deterministic inference — but this is an implementation constraint, not a definitional flaw in the rule itself (we can replace LLM with deterministic logic during our verification).
Reputation decay and motivational state depend on PnL feedback, which requires real trade execution — but this is part of the learning loop, not the core signal generation rule.

judge.reject_reason: Сигнал входа определяется решением LLM-модели (Chairman), которая обрабатывает неструктурированные текстовые ответы других LLM-аналитиков и риск-менеджеров. Статья не содержит детерминированного, воспроизводимого правила для получения финального сигнала: нет чёткой математической или логической формулы, преобразующей значения индикаторов в 'BUY'/'SELL' без промежуточного LLM-интерпретирования. Все описанные условия (например, '3 BLOCKED → hold unless analyst consensus is overwhelming (9+)') зависят от субъективной интерпретации LLM, а не от фиксированного алгоритма. Парсинг ответов аналитиков ('BUY/SELL/NO SIGNAL in 3 sharp sentences. No JSON.') не описан технически — нет регулярных выражений, правил извлечения или валидации; статья прямо указывает, что только Chairman отвечает в JSON, а остальные — в свободной форме. Это фатальный порок: невозможно записать полное детерминированное правило для проверки на закрытых барах.
judge.summary: Статья описывает архитектуру AI-хедж-фонда с ансамблем из 10 аналитиков и 4 риск-менеджеров, чьи голоса взвешиваются по репутации и объединяются через LLM-председателя для выдачи торгового сигнала. Однако финальное решение принимается непрозрачно через генерацию естественного языка и последующий парсинг JSON-ответа LLM, без детерминированного, формализованного правила, основанного исключительно на исторических данных и индикаторах.
